script.opening: "Hi — so, this is a bit awkward on a video call. My girlfriend basically forced me to book this. I found a little lump on one of my, you know, testicles a few weeks ago. It doesn’t hurt or anything, so I’m sure it’s nothing — probably just a cyst or I’ve tweaked something at the gym. I just want you to tell me it’s fine so she stops nagging. It IS fine, right?"

facts.text: If asked properly: firm, hard, PAINLESS lump arising FROM the body of the right testis (not separate/above it), noticed 3 weeks ago, possibly enlarging, with a dull dragging/heaviness that side. Painless + hard + part of the testis = the classic concerning picture for testicular cancer.
If history taken: had an undescended testis as a baby, surgically corrected (orchidopexy) — a known risk factor for testicular cancer. He doesn’t know this is relevant.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the bravado is fear: he has actually googled it, seen the word "cancer", and is privately terrified — both of dying and, very specifically, of losing a testicle and what it means for his masculinity, his fertility, and his relationship. He’s pushing for "it’s fine" because he can’t bear it not to be. The "girlfriend made me" framing is cover.

If reached gently: worried that if something IS wrong, surgery means he’s "half a man", can’t have kids, won’t be desirable. These unspoken fears, if unaddressed, can make young men delay or disengage.

Officially: quick reassurance to placate his girlfriend. What he needs: examination and a suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12: consider it for a non-painful enlargement or change in shape or texture of the testis), with an urgent scrotal ultrasound, delivered so he accepts it despite his fear, with the masculinity/fertility worries met honestly (treatment is highly effective; sperm storage exists).

ice.ideas: It’s probably a harmless cyst or a gym strain; it doesn’t hurt so it can’t be serious.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he’s googled it, seen "cancer", and is terrified; specifically frightened of losing a testicle, his fertility and his masculinity, so he minimises to make it not be real.
ice.expectations: Quick reassurance that it’s fine. What he actually needs: examination, a suspected cancer pathway referral under NICE NG12, with an urgent scrotal ultrasound, and his masculinity/fertility fears addressed honestly.

cues: "It doesn’t hurt so it’s nothing" — painlessness is exactly what makes a hard testicular lump concerning, not reassuring.
"Tell me it’s fine so she stops nagging" — bravado covering real fear; the girlfriend’s insistence is the reliable signal.
Hesitation about the future/fertility if treatment is mentioned — the masculinity fear waiting to be named.

checkpoints.text: Recognises a hard, PAINLESS lump arising from the testis as concerning for testicular cancer and does NOT accept "it doesn’t hurt so it’s nothing" — painlessness is typical of malignancy, not reassuring

States the NICE NG12 routes correctly as two separate recommendations: (1) a non-painful enlargement or change in shape or texture of the testis → consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for testicular cancer — his case; (2) unexplained or persistent testicular symptoms → consider a direct-access ultrasound scan. For his hard, painless, intratesticular lump the action is the suspected cancer referral (with an urgent scan), not a scan alone — restated as the action

Takes the relevant history and examines: distinguishes a lump within the testis from epididymal/extra-testicular causes (cyst, hydrocele, epididymo-orchitis), elicits the undescended-testis/orchidopexy risk factor, and arranges in-person examination promptly, offering a chaperone (GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones, 2024) (does not rely on a video impression, and does not let arranging the examination delay the referral)

Addresses the masculinity/fertility fears honestly: testicular cancer is one of the most treatable cancers with excellent cure rates; if surgery is needed it is usually removal of one testis with the other preserving function/fertility; SPERM STORAGE (cryopreservation) is offered before treatment that may affect fertility (NICE NG257); a prosthesis is available — directly countering the "half a man" fear

Considers the differential without false reassurance: yes it could be a benign cyst/epididymal lump, but the only safe way to know is examination + ultrasound on the urgent pathway, not phone reassurance
Hears the bravado as fear and the girlfriend’s insistence as the real reason; gently surfaces the googling and the specific worries rather than taking "it’s fine, right?" at face value
Validates how hard this is for a young man to raise, normalises it, and meets the fertility/masculinity fears with warmth and accurate information so he accepts the pathway

Safety-nets and follows up: arranges examination + urgent ultrasound/referral, explains timescales and what to expect, advises to return sooner if pain/swelling/systemic change, ensures he will attend (engages the girlfriend/support with consent), documents, and tracks the result

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you came, even if it took some persuading — and I want to be straight with you, because that respects you more than empty reassurance: the fact it DOESN’T hurt is actually the reason I take a hard lump on the testicle seriously. The harmless ones often ache or come and go; a firm, painless lump that’s part of the testicle is the kind we always check properly."

"So here’s what needs to happen. I need to examine you in person, and then arrange an urgent ultrasound scan of the testicle and a referral to the specialists on the suspected cancer pathway — you should be seen quickly and get an answer within 4 weeks (28 days). The NICE suspected cancer guideline, NICE NG12, covers exactly this. It isn’t me saying it’s cancer; it’s me making sure that if there’s anything to find, we find it fast."

"One thing from your history matters: you had an undescended testicle as a baby that was fixed with surgery. That slightly raises the chance of problems in that testicle later, which is another reason I want this looked at properly rather than over a video call."

"Can I gently say — I suspect you’ve already looked this up and scared yourself, and that the ‘girlfriend made me’ is partly cover for being worried. That’s completely human. And I’d guess part of the fear is what it might mean for you as a man — fertility, surgery, all of that. Let’s put those on the table, because the news there is genuinely good."

"If this did turn out to be cancer — and we don’t know that — testicular cancer is one of the most curable cancers there is, with very high success rates. If a testicle needs removing, the other one almost always keeps your hormones and fertility normal, and we can store sperm beforehand as a safety net, and even fit a natural-looking prosthesis. You would not be ‘half a man’. Far from it."

"Let’s get you booked for the examination and the scan. If meanwhile it becomes painful, swells, or you feel unwell, come back sooner. Bring your girlfriend if it helps — she clearly’s got your back. I’ll make sure the referral goes today and I’ll follow up the result with you. You wanted me to say it’s fine; what I’m doing instead is making sure you actually find out, quickly, and that whatever it is, you’re not facing it alone."

f.learning: A firm, PAINLESS lump arising from the body of the testis is testicular cancer until proven otherwise — and painlessness is the concerning feature, not a reassuring one. The NICE NG12 action is a suspected cancer pathway referral for a non-painful enlargement or change in shape or texture of the testis, with examination and an urgent scrotal ultrasound — the separate NG12 direct-access ultrasound route is for unexplained or persistent testicular symptoms — never phone reassurance; an undescended-testis/orchidopexy history is a genuine risk factor. The examinable hidden agenda is that the young man’s bravado ("my girlfriend made me", "it’s fine, right?") masks real fear — he has googled it, seen "cancer", and is specifically terrified of losing a testicle, his fertility, and his masculinity. The skill is to refuse the dismissal without crushing him, surface the fear and the girlfriend’s reliable insistence, examine and refer on the urgent pathway, and meet the masculinity/fertility fears with accurate good news (testicular cancer is highly curable; the remaining testis preserves function; sperm storage and prosthesis exist) so he engages rather than delays.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG257 (fertility preservation) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024)
knowledge.summary: A hard, painless lump in the body of the testis in a young man is testicular cancer until examination and ultrasound say otherwise. Painlessness is the worrying feature, not the comforting one.

points.t: NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for testicular cancer in men with a non-painful enlargement or change in shape or texture of the testis. Consider a direct-access ultrasound scan for unexplained or persistent testicular symptoms.

A lump that cannot be separated from the testis is the concerning finding. Lumps felt separately above or behind it (epididymal cyst), a swelling that transilluminates (hydrocele) or a “bag of worms” (varicocele) are usually benign — but only a hands-on examination can make that call.

Germ cell tumours usually present as a firm, painless swelling or a dragging heaviness. Pain with fever, dysuria or discharge points more to epididymo-orchitis. The absence of pain should raise, not lower, suspicion.
A history of undescended testis carries a higher risk of testicular cancer even after orchidopexy. A previous testicular tumour and a family history also count. Their absence never excludes it.
A video call cannot assess a scrotal lump. Arrange a face-to-face examination promptly, offer a chaperone, and do not delay the referral or scan if examination is hard to arrange.

Testicular cancer is one of the most curable solid cancers. After removal of one testis, the other usually maintains testosterone and fertility. NICE NG257 (March 2026, which replaced CG156): offer sperm cryopreservation before treatment that may affect fertility. A prosthesis can be offered at surgery.

dg.d: Opened with a free description of the lump; did not answer “it’s fine, right?” before gathering the facts.
Occupation and body image as a personal trainer, the relationship and plans for children, what he has read online.
Arranged face-to-face examination with a chaperone offered; direct-access ultrasound and suspected cancer referral per NICE NG12.
Intratesticular tumour versus epididymal cyst, hydrocele, varicocele and epididymo-orchitis, tested with targeted questions.
Asked about symptoms of spread (cough, breathlessness, back pain, weight loss); recognised painless intratesticular lump plus orchidopexy history as high suspicion.
Stated clearly that this needs testicular cancer ruling out urgently, without claiming a diagnosis over video.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

Addressed the undescended-testis history and the psychological load; offered reliable written information.
Named same-day return triggers, a date to chase the referral, and personal ownership of the result.

model.text: Hi Jordan, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for booking this — I know it isn’t the easiest thing to talk about on a screen. Tell me about the lump in your own words.
model.why: Open start that acknowledges the awkwardness without rushing him

model.text: Yeah, it’s a bit weird. My girlfriend made me book it. Found a little lump a few weeks back in the shower. Doesn’t hurt, so I’m sure it’s nothing — a cyst or I’ve tweaked something lifting. It is fine, right?
I can hear you’d love me to say yes. I’d rather give you a proper answer than a quick one, so let me ask a few things first, then I’ll tell you honestly what I think and what happens next. Okay?
model.why: Sets an agenda and signals honesty without dismissing his question

model.text: Go on then.
Which side is it, and when exactly did you first notice it?
Right side. About three weeks ago. I think it might be a bit bigger now, but I don’t know.
When you feel it, is the lump part of the testicle itself, or does it feel like a separate little ball sitting above or behind it?
It’s on it. Like part of it. It’s quite hard.
Any pain, tenderness, redness, a temperature, burning when you pass urine, or any discharge?
model.why: Screens for infection and inflammatory causes

model.text: No. Just a sort of dull heavy feeling on that side, a dragging. No pain as such.
Any injury down there? And have you had any cough, breathlessness, back pain or weight loss?
model.why: Checks trauma and features of spread

model.text: Nothing like that. I’m fit — I train people for a living.
One thing from your notes — you had an operation as a baby for a testicle that hadn’t come down. Do you know much about that?
Only that it was fixed. I was a baby. Why, does that matter?
It’s relevant, and I’ll explain why in a moment.
model.why: Flags significance honestly without alarming him mid-history

model.text: Can I ask — before you booked, had you looked any of this up online?
model.why: Opens the door to the hidden fear

model.text: …Yeah. Few times. Everything says cancer. Which is why I’m saying it’s a cyst.
That’s a very human thing to do. When you read that, what was the bit that frightened you most?
model.why: Explores the specific concern rather than general anxiety

model.text: Honestly? Losing it. Being half a bloke. Not being able to have kids. I want kids one day. I don’t even want to say it out loud.
Thank you for saying it. Lots of young men carry exactly that fear and never voice it, and I’m really glad you have, because there’s good information I can give you on every one of those points.
model.why: Validates and normalises the masculinity and fertility fear

model.text: Here’s my honest view. A hard lump that’s part of the testicle, that doesn’t hurt and may be growing, is exactly the kind we always check quickly. The lack of pain is actually why I take it seriously. Your childhood operation also slightly raises the chance of testicular problems later. It could still be something harmless — but I can’t tell you that from a video.
model.why: Explains why painlessness and the risk factor raise concern

model.text: So you think it’s cancer.

I think it needs ruling out properly, and fast. I need to examine you in person — I can see you here in the next day or two, with a chaperone if you’d like. Then there’s a national urgent pathway for exactly this: a scan of the testicle and a specialist appointment — you should be seen quickly and get an answer within 4 weeks (28 days).
model.why: Arranges face-to-face examination and the NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway

model.text: Four weeks at most. Right. And if it is?

Then the news is better than what you read. Testicular cancer is one of the most curable cancers there is. If a testicle needs removing, the other one normally keeps your hormones and fertility working. Before any treatment you’d be offered sperm storage as a back-up, and a prosthesis can be fitted so things look the same.
model.why: Gives accurate reassurance on cure, fertility, sperm storage and prosthesis

model.text: I didn’t know about the storage thing. That actually helps.
So the plan: an examination with me this week, and I’ll send the urgent referral and scan request today rather than wait. Does that feel doable around your clients?
model.why: Shares the plan and checks it fits his life

model.text: I’ll move people. Can my girlfriend come?

Absolutely. She clearly cares, and she was right to push you. You can tell her as much or as little as you like — it’s your information. Would it help if I sent you some reliable reading so you’re not back on random websites tonight?
model.why: Supports involvement of his partner while respecting confidentiality

model.text: Yeah, please. The stuff online was grim.

If before the appointments it becomes painful, swells quickly, or you get a cough, breathlessness or back pain, contact us the same day. If the hospital hasn’t been in touch within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it — and I’ll check the result myself.
model.why: Specific safety-net and ownership of the referral

model.text: Okay. Thanks. I was hoping you’d just say it’s nothing.
I know. What I can say is we’ll find out quickly and you won’t be dealing with it alone. What are you going to tell your girlfriend when we finish?
That I need to be checked this week and scanned quickly, and that even if it’s the worst, it’s very fixable and I can store sperm.
That’s exactly it. I’ll see you in clinic.
model.why: Closes warmly and confirms the next step

social.t: A personal trainer whose work centres on his body, who wants children one day. Fear of losing a testicle is about identity and the future, not only illness.
Young men often present late and minimise. A partner’s insistence is useful; engaging her with his consent can help attendance.

legal.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): explain why the examination is needed, obtain consent, offer a chaperone and record the discussion.
If he needs surgery or further treatment, a fit note covers time off. If he is self-employed there may be no sick pay; signpost to benefits advice early.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): recognise the limits of what can be assessed remotely. A scrotal lump needs a hands-on examination, arranged promptly.
Document the NICE NG12 criterion, send the referral the same day, and have a system to check he was seen and the scan was reported.

community.t: Orchid (male cancer charity) and Macmillan Cancer Support for information and helplines; NHS guidance on testicular self-examination.

redFlags: Hard, painless lump arising from the testis, possibly enlarging — NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway
Previous undescended testis (even after orchidopexy), previous testicular tumour, family history
Symptoms of spread: cough, breathlessness, haemoptysis, back pain, weight loss, breast swelling
psychosocial: Occupation and self-image as a personal trainer
Relationship, hopes for children, what he has told his girlfriend
What he has read online and how frightened he is beneath the bravado
ice: Idea: “It’s a cyst, or I’ve strained something at the gym.”
Concern: cancer, losing a testicle, infertility and feeling “half a man”
Expectation: a quick “it’s fine” to settle his girlfriend

playbook.diagnosis: A hard, painless intratesticular lump present for three weeks, possibly enlarging, in a 28-year-old with a history of undescended testis corrected by orchidopexy: testicular cancer must be excluded urgently. Benign causes remain possible but cannot be assumed without examination and ultrasound.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Most lumps down there are harmless, but the ones that are firm, part of the testicle and don’t hurt are the ones we always check quickly with a scan. That’s not me saying it’s cancer — it’s me making sure that if it is, it’s found early, when it’s very curable.”

management.reflectIce: “You came hoping I’d say it’s nothing, and I think underneath you’re scared about what it could mean for you as a man and for having kids. Let’s deal with both — the checks, and the facts on those fears.”
management.psychosocial: Invite his girlfriend if he wants; give reliable written information; acknowledge work and income worries if treatment is needed.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face examination this week with a chaperone offered
Same-day NICE NG12 suspected cancer referral and direct-access testicular ultrasound
Explain cure rates, preserved function of the other testis, sperm storage before treatment (NICE NG257) and prosthesis
safetyNet: Same-day contact if pain, rapid swelling, cough, breathlessness or back pain
Ring if no appointment within a week; GP checks the scan and clinic outcome

pitfalls.intro: This station is lost when the candidate is persuaded by his confidence. The lump is suspicious because it is painless; the man is minimising because he is frightened. Miss either and the station fails.

items.fail: Accepting “it doesn’t hurt” as reassuring and advising review in a few weeks.
items.why: A painless hard intratesticular lump meets the NICE NG12 testicular criterion; watchful waiting is unsafe management.
items.fix: Say it plainly: “No pain is exactly why I want this scanned quickly.” Then arrange examination and the suspected cancer pathway.

items.fail: Making a diagnosis or plan purely from the video, without arranging a face-to-face examination.
items.why: Distinguishing intratesticular from epididymal lumps needs palpation; relying on a remote impression is a recognised safety failure.
items.fix: Book an in-person examination within days with a chaperone offered — and send the referral and scan request in parallel so nothing waits.

items.fail: Not asking about, or not using, the orchidopexy history.
items.why: Undescended testis is a known risk factor; missing it looks like incomplete data gathering.
items.fix: Ask directly about childhood surgery, then use it in the explanation.

items.fail: Taking “my girlfriend made me come” at face value and never exploring his own worries.
items.why: Feedback: “did not identify or respond to cues”. The bravado is the cue.
items.fix: “Had you looked it up before booking? What worried you most?” — then pause and let him answer.

items.fail: Hearing the fear of losing a testicle or fertility and answering “let’s not get ahead of ourselves”.
items.why: Deferring the central fear feels dismissive and can drive avoidance of the referral.
items.fix: Give the facts now: high cure rates, the other testis usually preserves hormones and fertility, sperm storage before treatment, prosthesis.

items.fail: Using “two-week-wait” and “germ cell tumour” without explanation, then ending with “any questions?”.
items.why: Jargon and no check of understanding are standard failing feedback statements.
items.fix: Plain words — “an urgent scan and a specialist appointment, usually within two weeks” — and teach-back: “What will you tell your girlfriend?”

timeMap.d: He asks for “it’s fine, right?” in the first breath. Don’t answer yet — promise an honest answer after a few questions.
Side, duration, growth, inside versus separate from the testis, pain, infection features, trauma, symptoms of spread, and the orchidopexy history.
Ask what he read online and what scared him. The masculinity and fertility fear only surfaces if invited.
Painless and hard is the worrying feature. In-person examination this week, urgent NICE NG12 scan and referral sent today. Cure rates, the other testis, sperm storage, prosthesis.
Same-day triggers, chase date, you own the result. Teach-back: “What will you tell your girlfriend?”

wordPics.fail: Accepts “it doesn’t hurt so it’s nothing” and offers review if it grows; relies on a video impression; never asks about the orchidopexy; misses the fear beneath the bravado; no referral, or a referral with no explanation so he may not attend.
wordPics.pass: Recognises a painless hard intratesticular lump as suspicious; arranges examination and an urgent NICE NG12 pathway with ultrasound; notes the undescended-testis history; acknowledges he is worried; gives a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explicitly reframes painlessness; draws out the specific fear of losing a testicle and fertility and answers it with accurate facts (cure rates, the other testis, sperm storage, prosthesis); involves the girlfriend on his terms; owns the referral and result; teach-back confirms he will attend.

avoid.dont: “If it doesn’t hurt, it’s probably just a cyst — keep an eye on it.”
avoid.instead: “The fact it doesn’t hurt is actually why I want it checked quickly.”
avoid.why: Painless reassurance is the exact error that delays diagnosis of testicular cancer.

avoid.dont: “It could be cancer, so I’m referring you on the suspected cancer pathway.”
avoid.instead: “This needs ruling out quickly. I’ll examine you this week and arrange an urgent scan and specialist review.”
avoid.why: Blunt labelling without context frightens a young man who is already minimising, and he may not turn up.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry about fertility for now, let’s get the scan first.”
avoid.instead: “Even in the worst case, the other testicle usually keeps things working, and you’d be offered sperm storage first.”
avoid.why: Deferring his central fear leaves it to drive avoidance; accurate facts help him engage.

The lack of pain is actually why I take it seriously. Your childhood operation also slightly raises the chance of testicular problems later. It could still be something harmless — but I can’t tell you that from a video.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains why painlessness and the risk factor raise concern

SCA_MODELS.text: So you think it’s cancer.

I think it needs ruling out properly, and fast. I need to examine you in person — I can see you here in the next day or two, with a chaperone if you’d like. Then there’s a national urgent pathway for exactly this: a scan of the testicle and a specialist appointment — you should be seen quickly and get an answer within 4 weeks (28 days).
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges face-to-face examination and the NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway

SCA_MODELS.text: Four weeks at most. Right. And if it is?

Then the news is better than what you read. Testicular cancer is one of the most curable cancers there is. If a testicle needs removing, the other one normally keeps your hormones and fertility working. Before any treatment you’d be offered sperm storage as a back-up, and a prosthesis can be fitted so things look the same.
SCA_MODELS.why: Gives accurate reassurance on cure, fertility, sperm storage and prosthesis

SCA_MODELS.text: I didn’t know about the storage thing. That actually helps.
So the plan: an examination with me this week, and I’ll send the urgent referral and scan request today rather than wait. Does that feel doable around your clients?
SCA_MODELS.why: Shares the plan and checks it fits his life

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll move people. Can my girlfriend come?

Absolutely. She clearly cares, and she was right to push you. You can tell her as much or as little as you like — it’s your information. Would it help if I sent you some reliable reading so you’re not back on random websites tonight?
SCA_MODELS.why: Supports involvement of his partner while respecting confidentiality

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah, please. The stuff online was grim.

If before the appointments it becomes painful, swells quickly, or you get a cough, breathlessness or back pain, contact us the same day. If the hospital hasn’t been in touch within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it — and I’ll check the result myself.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net and ownership of the referral

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. Thanks. I was hoping you’d just say it’s nothing.
I know. What I can say is we’ll find out quickly and you won’t be dealing with it alone. What are you going to tell your girlfriend when we finish?
That I need to be checked this week and scanned quickly, and that even if it’s the worst, it’s very fixable and I can store sperm.
That’s exactly it. I’ll see you in clinic.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes warmly and confirms the next step

SCA_STEM.name: Jordan Eze
pmh: Undescended testis in infancy, corrected by orchidopexy
SCA_STEM.recent: No consultations on record for several years. Occupation: personal trainer.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video appointment booked by the patient: “lump on one testicle”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG257 (fertility preservation) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A hard, painless lump in the body of the testis in a young man is testicular cancer until examination and ultrasound say otherwise. Painlessness is the worrying feature, not the comforting one.

points.t: NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for testicular cancer in men with a non-painful enlargement or change in shape or texture of the testis. Consider a direct-access ultrasound scan for unexplained or persistent testicular symptoms.

A lump that cannot be separated from the testis is the concerning finding. Lumps felt separately above or behind it (epididymal cyst), a swelling that transilluminates (hydrocele) or a “bag of worms” (varicocele) are usually benign — but only a hands-on examination can make that call.

Germ cell tumours usually present as a firm, painless swelling or a dragging heaviness. Pain with fever, dysuria or discharge points more to epididymo-orchitis. The absence of pain should raise, not lower, suspicion.
A history of undescended testis carries a higher risk of testicular cancer even after orchidopexy. A previous testicular tumour and a family history also count. Their absence never excludes it.
A video call cannot assess a scrotal lump. Arrange a face-to-face examination promptly, offer a chaperone, and do not delay the referral or scan if examination is hard to arrange.

Testicular cancer is one of the most curable solid cancers. After removal of one testis, the other usually maintains testosterone and fertility. NICE NG257 (March 2026, which replaced CG156): offer sperm cryopreservation before treatment that may affect fertility. A prosthesis can be offered at surgery.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Opened with a free description of the lump; did not answer “it’s fine, right?” before gathering the facts.
Occupation and body image as a personal trainer, the relationship and plans for children, what he has read online.
Picked up “my girlfriend made me”, the online searching and the bravado as signals of fear, and explored them.
Idea (cyst or gym strain); concern (cancer, losing a testicle, fertility and masculinity); expectation (quick reassurance).
Arranged face-to-face examination with a chaperone offered; direct-access ultrasound and suspected cancer referral per NICE NG12.
Intratesticular tumour versus epididymal cyst, hydrocele, varicocele and epididymo-orchitis, tested with targeted questions.
Asked about symptoms of spread (cough, breathlessness, back pain, weight loss); recognised painless intratesticular lump plus orchidopexy history as high suspicion.
Stated clearly that this needs testicular cancer ruling out urgently, without claiming a diagnosis over video.
Examination this week, same-day referral and scan request, accurate information on cure, fertility, sperm storage (NICE NG257) and prosthesis.
Addressed the undescended-testis history and the psychological load; offered reliable written information.
Named same-day return triggers, a date to chase the referral, and personal ownership of the result.

social.t: A personal trainer whose work centres on his body, who wants children one day. Fear of losing a testicle is about identity and the future, not only illness.
Young men often present late and minimise. A partner’s insistence is useful; engaging her with his consent can help attendance.

legal.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): explain why the examination is needed, obtain consent, offer a chaperone and record the discussion.
If he needs surgery or further treatment, a fit note covers time off. If he is self-employed there may be no sick pay; signpost to benefits advice early.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): recognise the limits of what can be assessed remotely. A scrotal lump needs a hands-on examination, arranged promptly.
Document the NICE NG12 criterion, send the referral the same day, and have a system to check he was seen and the scan was reported.

community.t: Orchid (male cancer charity) and Macmillan Cancer Support for information and helplines; NHS guidance on testicular self-examination.

redFlags: Hard, painless lump arising from the testis, possibly enlarging — NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway
Previous undescended testis (even after orchidopexy), previous testicular tumour, family history
Symptoms of spread: cough, breathlessness, haemoptysis, back pain, weight loss, breast swelling
psychosocial: Occupation and self-image as a personal trainer
Relationship, hopes for children, what he has told his girlfriend
What he has read online and how frightened he is beneath the bravado
ice: Idea: “It’s a cyst, or I’ve strained something at the gym.”
Concern: cancer, losing a testicle, infertility and feeling “half a man”
Expectation: a quick “it’s fine” to settle his girlfriend

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: A hard, painless intratesticular lump present for three weeks, possibly enlarging, in a 28-year-old with a history of undescended testis corrected by orchidopexy: testicular cancer must be excluded urgently. Benign causes remain possible but cannot be assumed without examination and ultrasound.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Most lumps down there are harmless, but the ones that are firm, part of the testicle and don’t hurt are the ones we always check quickly with a scan. That’s not me saying it’s cancer — it’s me making sure that if it is, it’s found early, when it’s very curable.”

management.reflectIce: “You came hoping I’d say it’s nothing, and I think underneath you’re scared about what it could mean for you as a man and for having kids. Let’s deal with both — the checks, and the facts on those fears.”
management.psychosocial: Invite his girlfriend if he wants; give reliable written information; acknowledge work and income worries if treatment is needed.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face examination this week with a chaperone offered
Same-day NICE NG12 suspected cancer referral and direct-access testicular ultrasound
Explain cure rates, preserved function of the other testis, sperm storage before treatment (NICE NG257) and prosthesis
safetyNet: Same-day contact if pain, rapid swelling, cough, breathlessness or back pain
Ring if no appointment within a week; GP checks the scan and clinic outcome

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is lost when the candidate is persuaded by his confidence. The lump is suspicious because it is painless; the man is minimising because he is frightened. Miss either and the station fails.

items.fail: Accepting “it doesn’t hurt” as reassuring and advising review in a few weeks.
items.why: A painless hard intratesticular lump meets the NICE NG12 testicular criterion; watchful waiting is unsafe management.
items.fix: Say it plainly: “No pain is exactly why I want this scanned quickly.” Then arrange examination and the suspected cancer pathway.

items.fail: Making a diagnosis or plan purely from the video, without arranging a face-to-face examination.
items.why: Distinguishing intratesticular from epididymal lumps needs palpation; relying on a remote impression is a recognised safety failure.
items.fix: Book an in-person examination within days with a chaperone offered — and send the referral and scan request in parallel so nothing waits.

items.fail: Not asking about, or not using, the orchidopexy history.
items.why: Undescended testis is a known risk factor; missing it looks like incomplete data gathering.
items.fix: Ask directly about childhood surgery, then use it in the explanation.

items.fail: Taking “my girlfriend made me come” at face value and never exploring his own worries.
items.why: Feedback: “did not identify or respond to cues”. The bravado is the cue.
items.fix: “Had you looked it up before booking? What worried you most?” — then pause and let him answer.

items.fail: Hearing the fear of losing a testicle or fertility and answering “let’s not get ahead of ourselves”.
items.why: Deferring the central fear feels dismissive and can drive avoidance of the referral.
items.fix: Give the facts now: high cure rates, the other testis usually preserves hormones and fertility, sperm storage before treatment, prosthesis.

items.fail: Using “two-week-wait” and “germ cell tumour” without explanation, then ending with “any questions?”.
items.why: Jargon and no check of understanding are standard failing feedback statements.
items.fix: Plain words — “an urgent scan and a specialist appointment, usually within two weeks” — and teach-back: “What will you tell your girlfriend?”
